    2. 17.11  Which Functions Respect the Order

    17.11  Which Functions Respect the Order

    Chapter 13 §05 ended on two facts that sit awkwardly together. If A⪰B⪰O, then A1/2⪰B1/2 (Proposition 13.5.4); but A2⪰B2 can fail (Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order)). For numbers, both t↦t1/2 and t↦t2 are increasing on [0,∞), and both preserve inequalities. This section names the property that separates them and proves it for every function the book can reach. It then compares that property with what §02’s min–max theorem already gives for every increasing function, and states without proof the classification that settles the question. Since this is the last section of the chapter, it ends by summing up the chapter’s moves and listing the promises the chapter has paid.

    Throughout, F=R or F=C, and every matrix whose eigenvalues are indexed is Hermitian, with eigenvalues λ1(A)≥⋯≥λn(A) indexed decreasingly and repeated according to multiplicity. The letter I denotes an interval of real numbers (open, closed, or half-open, bounded or not). It is plain italic, and it is not the bold identity matrix I. A function f:I→R is increasing when s≤t implies f(s)≤f(t); strictness is not required. Every result below holds for either choice of F, with the same proof. No analysis is used anywhere in this section except in the last part, which states a theorem without proving it.

    17.11.1. Functions of a Hermitian matrix

    Chapter 12 §08 already applies a function to a matrix, and nothing needs rebuilding. Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian. The operator x↦Ax on Fn has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors (Corollary 12.4.3, Corollary 12.5.2), so it has a spectral resolution A=μ1P1+⋯+μkPk with μ1,…,μk the distinct eigenvalues and Pj the orthogonal projection onto the eigenspace of μj (Definition 12.8.1, Theorem 12.8.1). For any function f defined on spec(A), Definition 12.8.2 sets f(A):=f(μ1)P1+⋯+f(μk)Pk. In this section f is always defined on an interval I containing spec(A), and f(A) is formed from the restriction of f to the spectrum: the values of f off the spectrum play no part. Four facts from Theorem 12.8.3 are used constantly.

    • Polynomials give the expected answer (part (a)): t↦α+βt gives αI+βA, and t↦t2 gives A2.
    • Sums and products go through (part (b)): (f+g)(A)=f(A)+g(A), (cf)(A)=cf(A), and (fg)(A)=f(A)g(A).
    • Real-valued f gives a Hermitian f(A) (part (c)). This is what lets f(A) be compared with anything in the Loewner order.
    • The eigenvectors do not change (part (d)): f(A) has the same orthonormal eigenbasis as A.

    Two instances have names already. If 0∉spec(A), then t↦1/t gives A−1, as Chapter 12 §08 records right after Definition 12.8.2. If A⪰O, then t↦t1/2 gives the positive square root A1/2 of Theorem 13.2.1, which Chapter 13 §02 constructed in exactly this way.

    17.11.2. Operator monotone and operator convex functions

    Chapter 13 §05 introduced the Loewner order A⪰B, meaning A−B⪰O (Definition 13.5.1). With the functional calculus available, the natural question is which functions f carry A⪰B to f(A)⪰f(B).

    The obvious guess is “the increasing ones”, since that is the answer for numbers. It is wrong. The function t↦t2 is increasing on [0,∞), and Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order) gives Hermitian 2×2 matrices A⪰B⪰O with A2⪰̸B2. So the property we want is stronger than being increasing, and it needs its own name.

    A function is operator monotone when applying it to Hermitian matrices never breaks the Loewner order, at every size at once.

    Definition 17.11.1 (Operator Monotone and Operator Convex Functions)

    Let I⊆R be an interval and let f:I→R.

    • (a) f is operator monotone on I if, for every size n≥1 and every pair of Hermitian matrices A,B∈Mn(F) whose spectra lie in I, A⪰B⟹f(A)⪰f(B).
    • (b) f is operator convex on I if, for every size n≥1, every pair of Hermitian matrices A,B∈Mn(F) whose spectra lie in I, and every θ∈[0,1], f(θA+(1−θ)B)⪯θf(A)+(1−θ)f(B). It is operator concave on I if −f is operator convex on I.

    Here f(A) is the matrix of Definition 12.8.2.

    In words: the first condition takes any two Hermitian matrices of the same size with spectra inside the domain of f. If the first dominates the second, applying f must preserve that. The second condition is the matrix version of “the chord lies above the graph”. Both are infinitely many conditions, one for each size n. A function that passes the test for 2×2 matrices has not yet passed it for 3×3 ones. The clause “for every n” is why the notion is hard, and also why it is interesting.

    Everything in the definition makes sense. Since spec(A)⊆I, the matrix f(A) is defined, and it is Hermitian because f is real-valued (Theorem 12.8.3 (c)). So f(A)⪰f(B) is a statement about two Hermitian matrices, as Definition 13.5.1 requires. In (b) one more thing needs checking: the spectrum of C=θA+(1−θ)B must lie in I, or f(C) would not be defined. The matrix C is Hermitian. Let x be a unit eigenvector of C for the eigenvalue μ. Then μ=⟨Cx,x⟩=θ⟨Ax,x⟩+(1−θ)⟨Bx,x⟩. By Lemma 13.5.2, ⟨Ax,x⟩ lies in [λn(A),λ1(A)]. That interval is contained in I, because its endpoints are eigenvalues of A and I is an interval. Likewise ⟨Bx,x⟩∈I. So μ is a convex combination of two points of the interval I, and it therefore lies in I.

    The smallest size already says something, and the proof is three lines.

    Proposition 17.11.1 (Operator Monotone Functions Are Increasing)

    If f is operator monotone on I, then f is increasing on I.

    Proof. Let s≤t in I, and take n=1, A=(t), B=(s). These are Hermitian, their spectra {t} and {s} lie in I, and A−B=(t−s)⪰O. Hence f(A)⪰f(B), and since f(A)=(f(t)) and f(B)=(f(s)), this says f(t)−f(s)≥0. This shows that f is increasing.

    The converse is false, and the failure is the reason this section exists.

    Warning. Increasing is not enough. “Increasing” is exactly the case n=1 of the definition, and sizes n≥2 are where all the new content lies. The function t↦t2 is increasing on [0,∞) and is not operator monotone there. The 2×2 matrices A=(2111) and B=(1111) of Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order) satisfy A⪰B⪰O, yet A2−B2 has negative determinant. Chapter 13 §05 traced the failure to noncommutativity: the number proof factors a2−b2 as (a−b)(a+b), and for matrices that factorization needs AB=BA.

    Quick check. Is t↦t3 operator monotone on R when only n=1 is tested? What does the answer tell you about n=2?

    Solution. For n=1 the condition says only that f is increasing, as the proof of Proposition 17.11.1 shows, and t↦t3 is increasing on R. So it passes at n=1. That tells us nothing about n=2, where the test is genuinely new. In fact t↦t3 fails at n=2 (exercise C3).

    17.11.3. The examples we can prove

    Four families are within reach, and the first is the simplest. It includes a degenerate case, the constant functions, which respect every order because they flatten everything to one matrix.

    Proposition 17.11.2 (Increasing Affine Functions)

    Let α,β∈R with β≥0. Then f(t)=α+βt is operator monotone on R. Moreover, every affine function t↦α+βt, with β of either sign, is both operator convex and operator concave on R.

    Proof. By Theorem 12.8.3 (a), f(A)=αI+βA for every Hermitian A. Let A⪰B be Hermitian of the same size. Then f(A)−f(B)=β(A−B), and for every x, ⟨β(A−B)x,x⟩=β⟨(A−B)x,x⟩ ≥ 0, a product of two nonnegative numbers. Hence f(A)⪰f(B). For the second statement, with C=θA+(1−θ)B, f(C)=αI+βθA+β(1−θ)B=θ(αI+βA)+(1−θ)(αI+βB)=θf(A)+(1−θ)f(B), so the inequality in Definition 17.11.1 (b) holds with equality, for f and for −f alike.

    The second example is the one that behaves like the square root: t↦−1/t. For numbers, a≥b>0 gives −1/a≥−1/b because one may divide by the product ab. For matrices that division is unavailable, since A and B need not commute. Chapter 13 §05 already found the way round.

    Proposition 17.11.3 (The Negative Reciprocal Is Operator Monotone)

    The function t↦−1/t is operator monotone on (0,∞). Explicitly: if A,B∈Mn(F) are Hermitian with A⪰B≻O, then A≻O and −A−1 ⪰ −B−1,that is,B−1⪰A−1.

    Idea. A congruence removes the noncommutativity. Conjugating by B−1/2 turns B into I and A into C=B−1/2AB−1/2⪰I. Now one of the two matrices is the identity, which commutes with everything, so the argument for numbers applies to the eigenvalues of C: they are all ≥1, so those of C−1 are all ≤1. Undoing the congruence carries I⪰C−1 back to B−1⪰A−1. That is exactly the proof of Theorem 13.5.3 (d), so the proposition is that clause read as a statement about the function t↦−1/t.

    Proof. Let A⪰B be Hermitian with spectra in (0,∞). By Theorem 13.1.5 (b), a Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are all positive is positive definite, so B≻O. By Theorem 13.5.3 (d), A≻O and B−1⪰A−1. Put f(t)=−1/t. By Definition 12.8.2 and the instance t↦1/t recalled above, f(A)=−A−1 and f(B)=−B−1. Hence f(A)−f(B)=B−1−A−1 ⪰ O, which is the assertion. The size n was arbitrary, so f is operator monotone on (0,∞).

    Two things make the whitening work, and they are worth separating. First, once one of the two matrices is I, the comparison C⪰I can be settled eigenvalue by eigenvalue, because I commutes with everything. Second, inversion gets along with congruence: (S∗MS)−1=S−1M−1(S−1)∗ is again a congruence, and that is what carries the conclusion back from C to A. For a general f there is no such identity, since f(S∗MS) is usually not a congruence of f(M), so the argument does not simply transfer to other functions.

    To build more examples out of these, one needs to know which ways of combining functions preserve the property.

    Proposition 17.11.4 (Combining Operator Monotone Functions)

    Let f and g be operator monotone on I.

    • (a) For every c≥0 and every α∈R, the functions f+g and α+cf are operator monotone on I.
    • (b) For every s∈R, the translate t↦f(t+s) is operator monotone on the interval I−s={t−s:t∈I}.

    Proof.

    • (a) Let A⪰B be Hermitian of the same size with spectra in I. By Theorem 12.8.3 (b), (f+g)(A)−(f+g)(B)=(f(A)−f(B))+(g(A)−g(B)). Both brackets are ⪰O by hypothesis, and for every x the quadratic form of the sum is the sum of the two nonnegative quadratic forms. So the sum is ⪰O by Definition 13.1.1. Likewise, using (b) and (a) of the same theorem, (α+cf)(A)−(α+cf)(B)=c(f(A)−f(B)), whose quadratic form is c≥0 times a nonnegative one.

    • (b) Let g(t)=f(t+s) on I−s, and let A be Hermitian with spectrum in I−s, with spectral resolution A=∑jμjPj. By Theorem 12.8.1 (c) and (d), A+sI=∑j(μj+s)Pj, and the numbers μj+s are distinct. The Pj are nonzero self-adjoint idempotents with PiPj=O for i≠j and ∑jPj=I (Theorem 12.8.1 (b), (c)). So by Theorem 12.8.2 this is the spectral resolution of A+sI, whose spectrum {μj+s} lies in I. By Definition 12.8.2, applied to each side, f(A+sI)=∑jf(μj+s)Pj=g(A). Now if A⪰B with spectra in I−s, then (A+sI)−(B+sI)=A−B⪰O, and both shifted matrices have spectra in I. Hence g(A)=f(A+sI)⪰f(B+sI)=g(B).

    Combining the last two propositions produces a whole one-parameter family. It will reappear in the final part of the section as the building block of every operator monotone function.

    Corollary 17.11.5 (Shifted Reciprocals)

    For every s≥0, the function t↦−1/(t+s) is operator monotone on (0,∞). For every s>0, so is t⟼tt+s=1−st+s.

    Proof. By Proposition 17.11.3 and Proposition 17.11.4 (b), t↦−1/(t+s) is operator monotone on (0,∞)−s=(−s,∞). Every Hermitian matrix with spectrum in (0,∞) has spectrum in (−s,∞), so it is in particular operator monotone on (0,∞). For the second function, t/(t+s)=1+s⋅(−1/(t+s)) with s>0, so Proposition 17.11.4 (a) applies.

    The fourth example is the one that started the section, and it is already proved. By Proposition 13.5.4, A⪰B⪰O implies A1/2⪰B1/2. A Hermitian matrix has spectrum in [0,∞) exactly when it is ⪰O (Theorem 13.1.4 (b)), and A1/2 is f(A) for f(t)=t1/2. So Chapter 13 §05’s proposition says precisely that t↦t1/2 is operator monotone on [0,∞). It is not re-proved here. Its proof was a different kind of argument, an eigenvector of A1/2−B1/2 pushed to a contradiction, and it too never needs A and B to commute.

    A nonexample by minimal change. The function t↦t=t1 is operator monotone on [0,∞) by Proposition 17.11.2. Raise the exponent from 1 to 2. The function is still increasing, still a polynomial, and still satisfies the case n=1. What fails is the clause “for every n”, already at n=2, with the witness of Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order). Lowering the exponent from 1 to 12 instead keeps the property. Among the powers, then, the dividing line lies somewhere around the exponent 1. Chapter 13 §05 said where it lies exactly, and the last part of this section returns to that.

    Why “for every n”. Each size imposes its own condition, and the conditions differ. At n=1, t↦t2 passes on [0,∞) and at n=2 it fails. A definition at one fixed size would admit functions that break at the next size, and it would not say what the functional calculus does to matrices in general. Requiring every size at once makes the class small enough to classify completely, which is what Loewner’s theorem at the end of this section does. The name comes from the same place as the name of the order: both are Loewner’s.

    17.11.4. Eigenvalues move monotonically for every increasing function

    Operator monotonicity is a strong requirement, and a weaker one comes for free. §02 proved that the whole ordered list of eigenvalues respects the Loewner order: by Corollary 17.2.4, A⪰B implies λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i. That paid the debt Chapter 13 §05 recorded after Theorem 13.5.3, and it holds with no hypothesis on commuting. Composing with an increasing f keeps it, once one knows what f does to the ordered list of eigenvalues.

    Lemma 17.11.6 (The Eigenvalue List of an Increasing Function)

    Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with spec(A)⊆I, and let f:I→R be increasing. Then f(A) is Hermitian and λi(f(A))=f(λi(A))(i=1,…,n).

    Proof. The matrix f(A) is Hermitian by Theorem 12.8.3 (c). By Corollary 12.4.3 (over C) or Corollary 12.5.2 (over R), there is an orthonormal basis (q1,…,qn) of Fn with Aqi=λi(A)qi. Let A=∑jμjPj be the spectral resolution, and fix i. Exactly one of the distinct eigenvalues equals λi(A); call it μj0. Then qi lies in the eigenspace of μj0, which is the image of Pj0, so Pj0qi=qi. For j≠j0, the eigenspace of μj0 is orthogonal to that of μj (Theorem 12.8.1 (a)), so Pjqi=0. By Definition 12.8.2, f(A)qi=∑jf(μj)Pjqi=f(μj0)qi=f(λi(A))qi. Thus (q1,…,qn) is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors of f(A), and f(λ1(A)),…,f(λn(A)) is its list of eigenvalues with multiplicity. Since λ1(A)≥⋯≥λn(A) and f is increasing, this list is already in decreasing order. A decreasing list of all the eigenvalues with multiplicity is the list λ1(f(A))≥⋯≥λn(f(A)), so the two agree term by term.

    The lemma needs f increasing only for the order of the list. For a general f, the numbers f(λi(A)) are still the eigenvalues of f(A), but they may have to be re-sorted. Two lines now give the eigenvalue-level statement.

    Proposition 17.11.7 (Every Increasing Function Is Monotone on Eigenvalues)

    Let f:I→R be increasing, and let A,B∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with spectra in I and A⪰B. Then λi(f(A)) ≥ λi(f(B))for every i=1,…,n.

    Proof. By Corollary 17.2.4, λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i. Since f is increasing, f(λi(A))≥f(λi(B)). By Lemma 17.11.6, applied to A and to B, the two sides are λi(f(A)) and λi(f(B)).

    So the squaring map, which is not operator monotone, is nevertheless monotone on eigenvalues. The Chapter 13 witness shows both at once.

    Example (The Squares Are Not Ordered, but Their Eigenvalues Are)

    Let A=(2111) and B=(1111), the pair of Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order), for which A⪰B⪰O and A2⪰̸B2. Compute the eigenvalues of A2 and B2 and compare them index by index.

    Solution. From Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order), A2=(5332) and B2=(2222). The first has trace 7 and determinant 10−9=1, so its eigenvalues are the roots of x2−7x+1: λ1(A2)=7+352≈6.854,λ2(A2)=7−352≈0.146. The second has trace 4 and determinant 0, so λ1(B2)=4 and λ2(B2)=0. Index by index: 7+352≥4 because 35≥1, and 7−352≥0 because 49≥45. So λi(A2)≥λi(B2) for i=1,2, as Proposition 17.11.7 predicts for the increasing function t↦t2 on [0,∞). Nevertheless A2−B2 is not ⪰O.

    So for every increasing f, the eigenvalues of f(A) dominate those of f(B) one index at a time. What operator monotonicity adds is that the matrices are ordered, and the example shows that this is strictly more.

    Warning. Eigenvalues in order do not make matrices in order. It is tempting to read Proposition 17.11.7 as “almost” operator monotonicity. It is not, because λi(M)≥λi(N) for every i does not imply M⪰N. Take M=diag(1,0) and N=diag(0,1): they have the same eigenvalues 1≥0, yet M−N=diag(1,−1) is indefinite. The Loewner order sees the eigenvectors as well as the eigenvalues, and the eigenvalue list forgets them.

    17.11.5. Operator convexity, and where the two notions part

    Operator convexity is the second notion of Definition 17.11.1, and one might expect it to behave like operator monotonicity. It does not: the function that fails to be operator monotone turns out to be operator convex.

    Proposition 17.11.8 (The Square Is Operator Convex)

    The function t↦t2 is operator convex on R. Explicitly: for Hermitian A,B∈Mn(F) and θ∈[0,1], θA2+(1−θ)B2−(θA+(1−θ)B)2=θ(1−θ)(A−B)2 ⪰ O.

    Idea. For numbers, θa2+(1−θ)b2−(θa+(1−θ)b)2=θ(1−θ)(a−b)2, which is a variance. The matrix version of the expansion produces AB+BA where the number version has 2ab, and that is exactly the cross term of (A−B)2=A2−AB−BA+B2. So this time noncommutativity cancels itself out and costs nothing. The square of a Hermitian matrix is ⪰O, which finishes the proof.

    Proof. By Theorem 12.8.3 (a), the function t↦t2 sends a Hermitian matrix to its square, so the displayed identity is what Definition 17.11.1 (b) requires. Expanding, and keeping the order of every product, (θA+(1−θ)B)2=θ2A2+θ(1−θ)(AB+BA)+(1−θ)2B2. Subtracting this from θA2+(1−θ)B2, and using θ−θ2=θ(1−θ)=(1−θ)−(1−θ)2, θA2+(1−θ)B2−(θA+(1−θ)B)2=θ(1−θ)(A2−AB−BA+B2)=θ(1−θ)(A−B)2. The matrix D=A−B is Hermitian, so D2=D∗D⪰O by Theorem 13.1.4 (c). Since θ(1−θ)≥0, the quadratic form of θ(1−θ)D2 is nonnegative, which proves the inequality.

    The contrast is now complete, and it runs both ways.

    • t↦t2 is operator convex but not operator monotone on [0,∞): Proposition 17.11.8 and Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order).
    • t↦−1/t is operator monotone but not operator convex on (0,∞): Proposition 17.11.3, and at n=1 the scalar function −1/t is not even convex, since with a=1, b=3, and θ=12 the value at the midpoint is −12, above the chord’s −23.

    So neither notion implies the other. Each implies its scalar version (increasing, convex) by taking n=1, and they strengthen those versions in different directions. Exercise C2 adds that t↦1/t is operator convex on (0,∞), so −1/t is operator monotone and operator concave there.

    17.11.6. What is not proved here

    The question the section opened with has a complete answer, and this chapter does not prove it. Here is the statement, so that the reader knows what the answer looks like and which of the facts above are pieces of it.

    Theorem 17.11.9 (Loewner’s Theorem, Statement)

    Let f:(0,∞)→R. The following are equivalent.

    • (i) f is operator monotone on (0,∞).
    • (ii) There are α∈R, β≥0, and a positive measure ν on [0,∞) with ∫[0,∞)dν(s)1+s2<∞, such that for every t>0 f(t)=α+βt+∫[0,∞)(s1+s2−1t+s)dν(s).
    • (iii) f is the restriction to (0,∞) of a function that is analytic on C∖(−∞,0] and sends every point of the upper half-plane {z:Imz>0} to a point with nonnegative imaginary part.

    We do not prove this theorem here. Its proof needs complex analysis and some measure theory, which lie outside Chapter 16’s list (A1)–(A6); Chapter 21 proves it. Nothing in this chapter depends on it.

    Read (ii) against what was proved above. The functions it superposes are t↦−1/(t+s) for s≥0, the translates of −1/t that Corollary 17.11.5 showed to be operator monotone. The constants s/(1+s2) do not depend on t and are there only to make the integral converge. The term α+βt is Proposition 17.11.2. So the theorem says that the examples of this section are, in a precise sense, all the examples there are: every operator monotone function on (0,∞) is an increasing affine function plus a nonnegative superposition of shifted reciprocals. The easy direction, (ii) ⇒ (i), is essentially Proposition 17.11.4 applied to an integral rather than a finite sum. What this book lacks is the analysis that carries the Loewner order through an integral, which is not on the list (A1)–(A6) in Chapter 16’s introduction. The hard direction, (i) ⇒ (ii), is the classification itself.

    Condition (iii) answers the opening question in one line. For z in the upper half-plane, z1/2 (the branch that is positive on (0,∞)) halves the argument of z, so its argument stays between 0 and π/2 and z1/2 stays in the upper half-plane. The square doubles the argument, which can pass π. The square root keeps the upper half-plane, and the square folds it over.

    Quick check. Find a point z of the upper half-plane whose square has negative imaginary part.

    Solution. Take z=−1+i, with Imz=1>0. Then z2=1−2i+i2=−2i, with imaginary part −2<0. So z↦z2 fails condition (iii) of Theorem 17.11.9, consistently with Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order).

    The same test settles the powers t↦tp. For 0<p<1, the function zp multiplies the argument by p and keeps the upper half-plane, and indeed for t>0 (a standard integral, not proved here) tp=sin⁡pππ∫0∞sp−1tt+sds, a positive superposition of the functions t/(t+s) of Corollary 17.11.5. For p>1, the argument of zp passes π for some z in the upper half-plane, and the test fails. This is the dividing line at exponent 1 that Chapter 13 §05 announced. Both halves, that tp is operator monotone on (0,∞) for every p∈(0,1) and that it is not for any p>1, are proved in Chapter 21, with Loewner’s theorem. What is proved so far is the case p=12 (Proposition 13.5.4) and, by applying it repeatedly, the cases p=1/2k (exercise C1).

    17.11.7. Summary and transfer

    The chapter began with a list of eigenvalues that the book had been able to order since Chapter 13 without being able to describe. It ends with each eigenvalue described as an optimization, and with a set of comparison theorems that follow from that description. Five moves did the work, and each transfers beyond this chapter.

    • The dimension count. Two subspaces of an n-dimensional space whose dimensions add to more than n share a nonzero vector. This one line drives Courant–Fischer (Theorem 17.2.3) and Weyl’s inequalities (§03) directly, and through Courant–Fischer everything after them. Transfer: whenever an extremal problem over vectors has to be compared with a fixed subspace, count dimensions before computing anything.
    • Min–max. Describe a quantity as a minimum over subspaces of a maximum over vectors, and prove it with two inequalities of different characters: one exhibits a witness subspace and computes, and the other takes an arbitrary subspace and intersects it with a span of eigenvectors. Applying the result to −A gives the dual form for free. Transfer: a description that names no eigenvector is what makes two different matrices comparable. The same shape describes singular values (§09) and inertia (§10).
    • Compress and interlace. Restricting a Hermitian form to a subspace gives a smaller Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are trapped by the original’s: compressing to a k-dimensional subspace puts λi of the piece between λi and λi+n−k of the whole, which are consecutive when k=n−1. Deleting a row and column (§04), compressing to an orthonormal frame (§06) and deleting a row or a column of a rectangular matrix (§09) are all this move; adding a rank-one term (§05) reaches the same interlaced picture by a different route, the Loewner order together with Weyl’s rank bound. Transfer: to bound the spectrum of a piece, look for the whole of which it is a compression.
    • Perturb in order. Compare λi(A+E) with λi(A) index by index, never “each eigenvalue with its nearest neighbor”. For Hermitian perturbations the Lipschitz constant is 1 in the spectral norm, independent of n, of the gaps, and of the eigenvectors (§03). For singular values it needs no hypothesis on E at all (§09). Transfer: where the Jordan block of Chapter 16 §07 showed that eigenvalues of general matrices can move like ε1/k, the Hermitian and singular-value problems are perfectly conditioned. Reduce a question to one of them whenever possible.
    • Majorize. When the right comparison is between sums of the largest entries rather than individual ones, compare partial sums of decreasing rearrangements. The diagonal of a Hermitian matrix is majorized by its spectrum, and by the Schur–Horn theorem majorization describes the possible diagonals exactly (§08); and the Ky Fan and Lidskii sums (§§06–07) are of the same type. Transfer: a family of partial-sum inequalities indexed by k, together with equality of the totals, is a majorization in disguise, and writing it as one lets the whole family be used at once.

    Two supporting moves recur under these five: apply the result to −A, which turns every max–min into a min–max and every top-k statement into a bottom-k one, and reduce singular values to eigenvalues, through A∗A or the Hermitian dilation. This section also reused a move from Chapter 13 §05, whiten, then compare: use a congruence to make one of the two matrices I. It works for t↦−1/t because inversion turns a congruence into a congruence, and not for a general f.

    The chapter also paid a series of promises made in earlier chapters, some of them long ago.

    The promise Made in Paid by
    The maximization route to eigenvalues “returns in Chapter 17, where the Rayleigh quotient and the Courant–Fischer theorem describe every eigenvalue of a self-adjoint operator by optimization” Chapter 12 §02 §01 (The Rayleigh quotient) and §02 (The min–max theorem), Theorem 17.2.3
    “Chapter 17 characterizes the eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix as maxima and minima of ⟨Ax,x⟩ — at which point the test becomes the theory” Chapter 13 §13 §01 and §02, Theorem 17.2.3
    A⪰B gives λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i, not only i=1 and i=n as in Theorem 13.5.3 (b) Chapter 13 §05 §02, Corollary 17.2.4
    “The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix move by at most ‖E‖2 under a Hermitian perturbation” Chapter 16 §07 §03 (How far eigenvalues move), Weyl’s perturbation bound
    Lemma 13.11.2 is “the extreme case of a family of statements about sums of the largest eigenvalues” Chapter 13 §11 §06 (Subspaces and Sums of Eigenvalues), Ky Fan’s theorem, of which it is a special case
    The second half of the approximation theorem, in the spectral norm Chapter 13 §11 and Chapter 16 §08 §09 (The same theory for singular values), Eckart–Young in the spectral norm
    Interlacing of the zeros of consecutive orthogonal polynomials, “Chapter 17’s business” Chapter 11 §10 §04 (Deleting a row and a column): strict interlacing, through the bordered-matrix criterion
    The operator monotone functions named in Chapter 13 §05 Chapter 13 §05 §11: definition and first examples; ts, log⁡t, and Loewner’s theorem remain Chapter 21’s, as that section said

    Four earlier theorems also received second proofs from the variational side, each of which shows something the first proof did not. The positivity of principal submatrices of a positive semidefinite matrix now follows from interlacing (§04, Deleting a row and a column). Hadamard’s inequality Theorem 13.7.3 follows from AM–GM after a diagonal scaling, with Schur’s theorem supplying the equal totals (§08, The diagonal and the spectrum). Sylvester’s law of inertia Theorem 14.5.1 is now a statement about the dimensions of subspaces, with no basis in it (§10, Inertia, again and additively). And the block test Theorem 13.6.1 is now a consequence of inertia additivity (§10).

    Some things the chapter did not do. Bounds for the eigenvalues of non-Hermitian matrices under perturbation, beginning with Bauer–Fike, are Chapter 20’s. Chapter 21 has Loewner’s theorem with the powers tp, Schur-concave functions, the strongest form of Lidskii’s inequality, and Eckart–Young in every unitarily invariant norm. The variational principle itself, though, is now a tool the book can use without comment: an eigenvalue of a Hermitian matrix is a min–max, and comparison theorems follow from that.

    17.11.8. Exercises

    A. Check your understanding

    Exercise (A1)
    • (a) Define “f is operator monotone on I”, and say what the clause “for every n” ranges over.
    • (b) Explain why an operator monotone function is increasing, and name an increasing function that is not operator monotone.
    • (c) Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if f:I→R is increasing and A⪰B are Hermitian with spectra in I, then λi(f(A))≥λi(f(B)) for every i.
    • (d) Decide whether the following is correct, and justify your answer: if A,B are Hermitian of the same size and λi(A)≥λi(B) for every i, then A⪰B.
    • (e) Which of t↦t2 and t↦−1/t is operator monotone on (0,∞), and which is operator convex there?
    • (f) What does this section prove about Loewner’s theorem?

    Solution.

    • (a) For every n≥1 and all Hermitian A,B∈Mn(F) with spectra in I, A⪰B implies f(A)⪰f(B), where f(A) is formed by Definition 12.8.2 (Definition 17.11.1 (a)). The clause ranges over all matrix sizes: the implication must hold for 1×1, 2×2, 3×3, … matrices simultaneously.

    • (b) Taking n=1 gives f(t)≥f(s) whenever t≥s in I (Proposition 17.11.1). The function t↦t2 on [0,∞) is increasing and is not operator monotone (Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order)).

    • (c) Correct. This is Proposition 17.11.7: Corollary 17.2.4 orders the eigenvalues of A and B index by index, f preserves each inequality, and Lemma 17.11.6 identifies f(λi(A)) with λi(f(A)).

    • (d) Incorrect. diag(1,0) and diag(0,1) have the same eigenvalues, but their difference diag(1,−1) is indefinite, so neither dominates the other.

    • (e) t↦−1/t is operator monotone on (0,∞) (Proposition 17.11.3) and is not operator convex, since already the scalar function is not convex: at 1, 3, and their midpoint 2, −12>12(−1−13)=−23. t↦t2 is operator convex (Proposition 17.11.8) and not operator monotone on (0,∞). The witness of Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order) has 0 in the spectrum of B, but the pair A=(3111)⪰B=(2111)≻O works: A2−B2=(5110) has determinant −1.

    • (f) Only the statement (Theorem 17.11.9) and the fact that its building blocks t↦−1/(t+s) are operator monotone (Corollary 17.11.5). The theorem itself is proved in Chapter 21.

    B. Practice

    Exercise (B1: Which are operator monotone?)

    Determine which of the following functions are operator monotone on the interval given. Justify your answer.

    • (i) f(t)=5+4t on R.
    • (ii) f(t)=3−2t on R.
    • (iii) f(t)=2−3t+1 on (0,∞).
    • (iv) f(t)=tt+2 on (0,∞).
    • (v) f(t)=t2 on [0,∞).

    Solution.

    • (i) Operator monotone, by Proposition 17.11.2 with β=4≥0.

    • (ii) Not operator monotone. It is not increasing, since f(1)=1<3=f(0), so it fails at n=1 with A=(1)⪰B=O1; compare Proposition 17.11.1.

    • (iii) Operator monotone. By Corollary 17.11.5 with s=1, t↦−1/(t+1) is operator monotone on (0,∞), and f=2+3⋅(−1/(t+1)) with 3≥0, so Proposition 17.11.4 (a) applies.

    • (iv) Operator monotone, by Corollary 17.11.5 with s=2>0.

    • (v) Not operator monotone: Example (Squaring does not preserve the Loewner order) gives A⪰B⪰O, with spectra {(3±5)/2} and {0,2} in [0,∞), and A2⪰̸B2.

    Exercise (B2: One pair, three functions)

    Let A=(3111),B=(2111).

    • (a) Show that A⪰B≻O.
    • (b) Compute A−1 and B−1, and verify directly that B−1⪰A−1, as Proposition 17.11.3 predicts.
    • (c) Show that A2⪰̸B2 by exhibiting a vector x with x⊤(A2−B2)x<0.
    • (d) Compute the eigenvalues of A2 and B2, and verify that λi(A2)≥λi(B2) for i=1,2. Hence explain which result of this section (c) and (d) illustrate together.

    Solution.

    • (a) A−B=diag(1,0), a diagonal matrix with nonnegative entries, so A−B⪰O and A⪰B. The leading principal minors of B are 2 and 2−1=1, both positive, so B≻O by Sylvester’s criterion (Theorem 13.1.5 (d)).

    • (b) detA=2 and detB=1, so A−1=12(1−1−13),B−1=(1−1−12),B−1−A−1=12(1−1−11). For every x∈R2, x⊤(B−1−A−1)x=12(x1−x2)2≥0, so B−1⪰A−1.

    • (c) A2=(10442) and B2=(5332), so A2−B2=(5110), with determinant −1<0. With x=(1,−3), x⊤(A2−B2)x=5+2⋅(1)(−3)+0=−1<0.

    • (d) A2 has trace 12 and determinant (detA)2=4, so its eigenvalues are 6±32=6±42, approximately 11.657 and 0.343. B2 has trace 7 and determinant 1, so its eigenvalues are (7±35)/2, approximately 6.854 and 0.146. For i=1, 12+82≥7+35 because 82>35. For i=2, 12−82≥7−35 is 5+35≥82. Both sides are positive, and squaring gives 70+305≥128, that is 5≥2915, which holds because 5≥841225. Hence (c) and (d) together illustrate Proposition 17.11.7 and the warning after it: the increasing function t↦t2 orders the eigenvalues but not the matrices.

    Exercise (B3: The convexity identity in numbers)

    With A and B as in B2 and θ=12, compute M=12A2+12B2−(12A+12B)2 directly, confirm that M=14(A−B)2, and hence conclude that (12(A+B))2⪯12(A2+B2).

    Solution. From B2, 12A2+12B2=12(15774)=(15/27/27/22). Next 12(A+B)=(5/2111), whose square is (254+152+152+11+1)=(29472722). Hence M=(15/2−29/4000)=diag(14,0). On the other side, A−B=diag(1,0), so 14(A−B)2=diag(14,0)=M, as Proposition 17.11.8 says with θ(1−θ)=14. Since diag(14,0) is diagonal with nonnegative entries, M⪰O, which is the displayed inequality.

    C. Going deeper

    Exercise (C1: Iterated square roots)
    • (a) Let A⪰B⪰O. Prove that A1/4⪰B1/4, where A1/4 is f(A) for f(t)=t1/4 on [0,∞).
    • (b) Deduce that t↦t1/2k is operator monotone on [0,∞) for every integer k≥0.
    • (c) Explain why the argument of (b) cannot reach t↦t3/4, and say where the operator monotonicity of tp for every p∈(0,1) is proved.

    Hint for (a): the positive square root is unique.

    Solution.

    • (a) Let g(t)=t1/4 on [0,∞). Since A⪰O, its spectrum lies in [0,∞) (Theorem 13.1.4 (b)), and g(A)=∑jμj1/4Pj is Hermitian with nonnegative eigenvalues by Theorem 12.8.3 (c) and (d), so g(A)⪰O. By Theorem 12.8.3 (b), g(A)2=(g2)(A), and g2(t)=t1/2, so g(A)2=A1/2. By the uniqueness in Theorem 13.1.4 (d), applied to A1/2⪰O, g(A) is the positive square root of A1/2: A1/4=(A1/2)1/2. The same holds for B. Now Proposition 13.5.4 applied to A⪰B⪰O gives A1/2⪰B1/2, and B1/2⪰O by Theorem 13.2.1. Applying Proposition 13.5.4 again, to A1/2⪰B1/2⪰O, gives (A1/2)1/2⪰(B1/2)1/2, that is A1/4⪰B1/4.

    • (b) Induction on k. For k=0 the function is t↦t, operator monotone by Proposition 17.11.2. Suppose A1/2k⪰B1/2k whenever A⪰B⪰O. The argument of (a), with t1/2k+1 in place of t1/4 and t1/2k in place of t1/2, shows that A1/2k+1=(A1/2k)1/2, and similarly for B. Both A1/2k and B1/2k are ⪰O, so Proposition 13.5.4 applied to A1/2k⪰B1/2k⪰O gives A1/2k+1⪰B1/2k+1.

    • (c) Each step of (b) takes a square root, which halves the exponent. Starting from 1, the exponents reached are exactly 1,12,14,…, and 34 is not among them. The operator monotonicity of tp for every p∈(0,1) needs a new idea, an integral representation of the kind in Theorem 17.11.9, and it is proved in Chapter 21.

    Exercise (C2: The reciprocal is operator convex)
    • (a) Let G∈Mn(F) with G≻O. Prove that the 2n×2n matrix (GInInG−1) is Hermitian and ⪰O.
    • (b) Let A,B≻O be of the same size and θ∈[0,1]. Prove that (θA+(1−θ)B)−1 ⪯ θA−1+(1−θ)B−1, that is, t↦1/t is operator convex on (0,∞).
    • (c) Deduce that t↦−1/t is both operator monotone and operator concave on (0,∞).

    Hint: Schur complements.

    Solution.

    • (a) G is Hermitian, and so is G−1, since (G−1)∗=(G∗)−1=G−1. The off-diagonal blocks are In and In∗=In, so the block matrix MG is Hermitian. Its corner G is ≻O, and its Schur complement is MG/G=G−1−In∗G−1In=O⪰O. By Theorem 13.6.1 (b), MG⪰O.

    • (b) Put C=θA+(1−θ)B. For x≠0, ⟨Cx,x⟩=θ⟨Ax,x⟩+(1−θ)⟨Bx,x⟩. Both inner products are >0, and θ and 1−θ are ≥0 and not both zero, so the sum is >0. Thus C≻O. By (a), MA⪰O and MB⪰O, so for every y∈F2n the quadratic form of θMA+(1−θ)MB=(CInInθA−1+(1−θ)B−1) is θ⟨MAy,y⟩+(1−θ)⟨MBy,y⟩≥0, and this block matrix is ⪰O. Its corner C is ≻O, so Theorem 13.6.1 (b) gives θA−1+(1−θ)B−1−C−1 ⪰ O, which is the claim. Since t↦1/t sends a positive definite matrix to its inverse (Definition 12.8.2), and a Hermitian matrix has spectrum in (0,∞) exactly when it is ≻O (Theorem 13.1.5 (b)), this is Definition 17.11.1 (b) for f(t)=1/t.

    • (c) Operator monotone by Proposition 17.11.3. Operator concave by definition, because its negative t↦1/t is operator convex by (b).

    Exercise (C3: The cube needs its own witness)
    • (a) With A and B as in B2, show that A3⪰̸B3. Conclude that t↦t3 is not operator monotone on [0,∞).
    • (b) One might hope to deduce (a) from the failure of t↦t2. Suppose t↦t3 were operator monotone on [0,∞). Applying it and t↦t1/2 (Proposition 13.5.4) to both sides of A⪰B⪰O, repeatedly and in any order, yields inequalities Aq⪰Bq for certain exponents q. Show that every such q has the form 3j/2k with integers j,k≥0, and that 2 never has this form. Explain why this means (a) needed a witness of its own.

    Solution.

    • (a) From B2, A⪰B⪰O, with spectra in (0,∞). Multiplying the squares of B2 once more, A3=(3414146),B3=(13885),A3−B3=(21661). The determinant is 21−36=−15<0, so the difference is indefinite. Explicitly, with x=(1,−5), x⊤(A3−B3)x=21+2⋅6⋅(−5)+25=−14<0. By Theorem 12.8.3 (a), t↦t3 sends A to A3, so it is not operator monotone on [0,∞).

    • (b) Start from A=A30/20. Taking the square root of Aq gives Aq/2, and cubing it gives A3q, by Theorem 12.8.3 (b) and the uniqueness of the positive square root, as in C1 (a); likewise for B. If q=3j/2k, the results are 3j/2k+1 and 3j+1/2k, of the same form. By induction on the number of steps, every exponent reached has the form 3j/2k. If 2=3j/2k, then 3j=2k+1, and the left side is odd while the right side is even, since k+1≥1. So no exponent reached equals 2. The hypothetical operator monotonicity of the cube therefore cannot be converted, by these means, into that of the square. The failure of the square does not formally imply the failure of the cube, and (a) had to find a pair of matrices of its own.
